papers.title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
papers.abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.

papers.title: Decentralized Bi-Level Optimization for Cooperative Orbital Transportation of a Rigid Payload
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of the space economy, alongside increasing orbital congestion and debris, is driving demand for reliable on-orbit transportation of large and non-cooperative objects. Performing such transportation with a swarm of small spacecraft distributes risk and removes the single point of failure inherent to monolithic architectures, but requires solving a non-convex trajectory optimization coupling every agent's cone-constrained thrust to the payload's rotational dynamics. Existing approaches span decentralized control laws with asymptotic guarantees but limited constraint enforcement, and centralized and partially centralized planners that reintroduce a single point of failure. In this work, we present a decentralized bi-level framework driven by exact gradients: the problem is split into an inner convex thrust allocation and an outer search over payload torque trajectories. This decomposition yields fuel-efficient solutions quickly, without requiring full NLP convergence, and at short timescales its performance scales with the number of agents. Theoretical convergence guarantees are established, and the method is validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulation, including closed-loop recovery from in-flight faults. These properties make the framework well suited to spacecraft swarm applications.

papers.title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.

papers.title: Structure-preserving reduced-order models of thin panels in supersonic and hypersonic flow
papers.abstract: We build structure-preserving reduced-order models for both challenge problems of the AePW-4 High-Speed Working Group. They are a clamped thin panel at Mach 1.92 (RC-19) and a cantilever plate at Mach 5.85 (HyMAX). The published data for each case hold no time-resolved response and no repeated runs. The physics must therefore be carried by the form of the model. One construction gives two models per problem. A Ritz-Galerkin reference model describes the plate. A learned model keeps the reference model's exact potential, fits the remaining generalized forces, and trains only a dissipation that cannot add energy. Its energy balance holds for any weights by construction. On the trained model the worst relative residual is 2.2e-15. On RC-19, shock relations predict a pressure ratio of 1.521 across the panel. Pressure-sensitive paint measured the same value. Thirty runs of the learned model place the mean dominant frequency within 1.0% of the measured 236 Hz. At one periodic and one chaotic condition, the learned model reproduces the response regime of a published reduced-order model in all sixteen runs. It does so without that model's 113 Hz spectral peak, which the measurements do not show. Measured displacements can also correct the chaotic response through one more force that respects the energy balance. We tested this on synthetic data at the experiment's 5 kHz sampling rate. The state error is 1.25% of the panel thickness without noise and 3.5% with 10 micrometers of noise. On HyMAX the learned model follows the reference model's trailing-edge displacement for 65 ms with a relative error of 3.7%. These results show that a model whose structure carries the physics can match measured flutter behavior when the available data cannot train it.

papers.title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
papers.abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

papers.title: RheOPT: Few-Shot Non-Newtonian Flow Prediction via Newtonian Pretraining of RheOFormer
papers.abstract: Despite advances in numerical methods, non-Newtonian flow simulations remain computationally expensive because velocity and stress must be advanced together through rate- and history-dependent constitutive dynamics. Neural-operator surrogates reduce inference cost after training, but their training data require the same expensive simulations they aim to replace, making data-efficient learning essential when only a few non-Newtonian simulations can be afforded. Here, we introduce the Rheological Operator Pretrained Transformer (RheOPT), which pretrains a transformer-based neural operator on inexpensive Newtonian simulations and fine-tunes it on a small number of non-Newtonian samples. Rather than transferring the Newtonian constitutive response itself, RheOPT reuses geometry-conditioned transport structure that remains useful after the stress model changes. We evaluate RheOPT in two geometry-matched settings: a $4{:}1$ contraction channel for Giesekus, Oldroyd-B, and Bingham fluids, and the oscillatory wake behind a triangular obstacle for Oldroyd-B flow. In the contraction, Newtonian pretraining substantially improves few-shot prediction, and a model fine-tuned on four target samples can match or exceed a from-scratch model trained on four times as many. This benefit is reliable under reversible instance normalization (RevIN) but dataset dependent under Global normalization, a difference we trace to the dynamic range of each fluid's velocity and stress fields. In the wake, where relative $L_2$ error alone cannot verify that vortex shedding is recovered, phase-insensitive diagnostics show that pretraining recovers the shedding frequency and wake fluctuation amplitude that are suppressed by the from-scratch model in the few-shot regime. Overall, RheOPT establishes Newtonian simulation as a physically grounded pretraining source for data-efficient non-Newtonian operator learning.

papers.title: Metric Conformal Prediction via the Conditional Expected Local Radius
papers.abstract: We introduce the conditional expected local radius (CELR) and develop a new conformal prediction method for non-Euclidean responses in general metric spaces. CELR measures local conditional probability concentration, allowing prediction sets to accommodate heterogeneity and multimodality without requiring densities or a vector space structure. Its conditional distribution yields a nonconformity score that is comparable across covariate values and avoids costly transport comparisons between distance profiles. We further adapt a metric distributional random forest that handles multivariate covariates and nonlinear interactions, while a single forest fit supplies all score components, reducing computation by eliminating repeated local fitting. We establish uniform consistency of the estimators and asymptotic conditional validity under suitable regularity conditions, together with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability. Numerical studies demonstrate effective uncertainty quantification across different metric spaces and substantial computational savings over the conditional profile score method.

papers.title: Sketching Outside the Hilbert Space for the Infinite-Dimensional Randomised SVD
papers.abstract: In randomised numerical linear algebra, common choices for distributions of sketch vectors $ω\in \mathbb R^n$ are isotropic, so that $\mathbb E[ωω^T]=I_n$. Unfortunately, the natural extension of an isotropic vector in $(\mathbb R^n, \|\cdot \|_{2})$ to an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ may not exist as an element of the space, posing an obstacle for any attempt to lift the randomised SVD to infinite-dimensional target operators $A$. Current workarounds either forego isotropy and take $ω$ to be a continuous Gaussian process with trace-class covariance operators, or leave $ω$ implicit by instead sampling $Aω$ as if $ω$ were isotropic Gaussian. We unify their approaches by introducing "sketch functionals", an example of cylindrical random variables (Vakhania--Tarieladze--Chobanyan 1987) which allow us to treat general, non-Gaussian distributions with bounded covariance operators. To demonstrate the utility of the new theory, we apply it to develop novel bounds for the infinite-dimensional randomised SVD with a general class of sub-Gaussian sketch distributions.

papers.title: QuaNAS: Uncertainty-Aware Reuse of Earlier Searches for Query-Efficient Neural Architecture Search
papers.abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) on a new dataset often affords only tens of short training runs, so what the search knows before its first evaluation decides its efficiency. Yet most NAS methods start from scratch, guided at best by zero-cost proxies that are unreliable across tasks. QuaNAS treats a library of earlier searches in the same search space as explicit knowledge of uncertain reliability. Main effects of design decisions learned from this library and, secondarily, zero-cost proxies become priors over candidate architectures without any label of the new dataset. A Gaussian process starts at the prior optimum and re-estimates after every evaluation how far each prior is trusted. Under a protocol frozen before any confirmation data were seen, QuaNAS was evaluated once on 12 new image, time-series, text and tabular datasets. It lowered anytime regret on the short-training objective 2.7- to 3.9-fold relative to five pre-specified NAS baselines that start from scratch (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0012 each). Its final models matched (non-inferiority margin 0.5 pp) or exceeded matched-recipe reference models on nine datasets, as did the prior optimum, selected without a single evaluation. Post-hoc comparisons with established transfer methods given the same library trace the gain to the library: without it, the same Gaussian process had over twice the regret. They also show where each transfer mechanism works best: the pooled main effects of QuaNAS for weakly transferable tabular tasks, per-task surrogates for image, time-series and text tasks and for small or mismatched libraries. Finally, the main effects make the transferred knowledge inspectable.

We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

papers.title: In-Context Learning World Models for Robot Dual-Arm Manipulation of Soft Garment with Partial Observations
papers.abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.

Every trip ends in a receipt, so a layout, price, pack or promotion can be tried on the same shoppers before it reaches the store. Around this core, TwinStore provides 3D playback, paired comparisons and layout optimization, shopper interviews, a trade-area model, counterfactual edits of real shelf photos, a marketing studio with eleven tools, and an assistant that turns a plain sentence into a drafted study or an answer grounded in a run's own numbers. In a held-out validation on eleven public datasets, simulated receipts approach the households' own natural variation (category-mix divergence 0.017--0.018 against a real drift of 0.012), price elasticities fall inside the range measured in the field, and three independent decision models agree. TwinStore runs on cloud or on-device models and is distributed with installers for Windows, macOS and Linux.

However, existing approaches are limited to a few dozen preselected adapters and require expensive image generation in every interaction round. We introduce HimmBO, a two-stage method that scales preference-driven adapter merging to much larger collections while reducing image-generation cost. Its screening stage recovers the active adapter set through level-set estimation over pre-generated images, requiring no image generation. The refinement stage then optimizes merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace. Both stages use a style-aware kernel, allowing preference information to transfer between visually similar adapters. In simulated-user image-matching experiments, HimmBO achieves higher final similarity than all comparisons while reaching a given similarity with under one tenth of the image generations required by prior work. Its performance remains stable as the collection grows to 1080 adapters, while competing methods degrade substantially.

papers.title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
papers.abstract: Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain. State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings. We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations. Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost. Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively. A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation. Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90\% on different terrains, compared with below 40\% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations. Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.

papers.title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.

papers.title: An Introduction to World Models for Generalist Agents
papers.abstract: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.

papers.title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history.   Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.

papers.title: Evaluating Type-1 Diabetes Digital Twins by Decision Quality
papers.abstract: A digital twin (DT) for type 1 diabetes (T1D) can predict how an individual's blood glucose will respond to different insulin treatments without actually trying them. For each treatment, downstream statistics of predicted glucose trajectories, such as glycemic risk, can be computed to guide clinical decisions. However, the quality of DTs is usually measured by the accuracy of their predicted glucose trajectories, which may not reflect the quality of the downstream treatment decisions they inform. In this work, we directly evaluate DTs by this decision quality on downstream treatment ranking, i.e., whether a DT predicts glucose trajectories that can be used to rank candidate treatments as the real patient would. We present an evaluation protocol over 30 virtual patients from the FDA-accepted UVA/Padova model, each simulated under 21 different basal-bolus treatments. For each patient, a DT is fitted under one treatment and then produces glucose trajectories for the remaining 20 treatments. Our results show that prediction accuracy and decision quality disagree. papers.title: Numerical Analysis Applications in Improving Engineering Models
papers.abstract: Numerical analysis serves as the fundamental pillar of modern engineering modeling, providing the mathematical and computational tools necessary to transform complex physical equations into practical numerical solutions. This study reviews contemporary applications of numerical analysis in enhancing engineering models, focusing on methodological advancements in solving partial differential equations, data-driven model order reduction techniques, adaptive mesh methods, and machine learning-based surrogate models. The study employs a synthetic analytical approach that combines a review of recent literature with an analysis of empirical results from various numerical methods, addressing hybrid models that integrate traditional techniques with artificial intelligence. The analysis demonstrates that combining traditional numerical analysis methods with artificial intelligence and reduced-order models has revolutionized the ability of engineers to simulate complex multiphysics systems with unprecedented accuracy and computational efficiency; hybrid models have achieved computational speedups ranging from 72 to 522 times compare to traditional methods. Furthermore, the study addresses challenges related to computational cost and solution sensitivity to initial conditions, examining cutting-edge innovative solutions such as physicsinformed neural networks and causality-based learning. The study concludes that future trends in this field are shifting towards the development of hybrid models that combine analytical accuracy with computational speed, with an increasing emphasis on generalization capabilities beyond the training data. This opens up broad prospects for digital engineering and digital twin applications across the industrial, energy, and infrastructure sectors. The study offers a comprehensive perspective on the development of engineering models using advanced numerical analysis techniques and identifies promising future research directions in this vital field.

papers.title: Advances and Prospects of Biodegradable Magnesium-based Metal Matrix Composites for Biomedical Implants: A Comprehensive Review
papers.abstract: Magnesium-based biodegradable composites offer significant advantages over nondegradable materials for biomedical implants. These materials degrade gradually in physiological environments, thereby reducing stress shielding and eliminating the need for secondary implant removal surgeries. This review explores how alloying elements (e.g., Zn, Ca, Sr) in the magnesium matrix and reinforcing phases (e.g., hydroxyapatite, SiC, TiC) in metal matrix composites influence degradation kinetics, mechanical integrity, and ion release behaviour. Proper regulation of the degradation rate is critical for maintaining mechanical support during the healing phase while ensuring biocompatibility. This study expands the use of magnesium composites in implantable medical devices. Some examples are orthopaedic implants, circulatory stents, bone fixation devices, and soft tissue scaffolds. The above uses demonstrate the ability of magnesium composites to improve patient outcomes and reduce implant-related procedures through gradual breakdown and tissue regeneration. The review also reports the biodegradation control, biocompatibility, manufacturing scale-up, and regulatory requirements for clinical translation. Successful commercialisation depends on balancing the degradation rate with mechanical support, limiting cytotoxicity, and meeting regulatory standards. In conclusion, magnesium-based biodegradable composites have the potential to revolutionise biomedical implants. The unique combination of mechanical properties, biocompatibility, and regulated biodegradation improves patient outcomes and therapy efficacy. Medical device design and regenerative medicine will benefit from magnesium composites as researchers improve synthesis methods, material properties, and overcome barriers.

papers.title: Equivariant deep neural networks under finite group for solving partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Incorporating properties of partial differential equations (PDEs) or their solutions into the loss function of physics-informed neural networks (PINN) is a common strategy to improve its performance, yet it frequently introduces difficulties associated with multi-objective optimization. In this paper, we embed the finite group of either PDEs or their solutions directly into the network architecture and construct an equivariant deep neural network (eDNN) for solving PDEs, whose architecture is inherently equivariant under the corresponding finite group. Specifically, we propose a general framework for the eDNN under the finite groups with linear transformations on the dependent variables, and also design an explicit network architecture for a nonlinear finite group. As a result, the proposed eDNN exhibits enhanced learning performance and extrapolation capability. Numerical experiments verify that the eDNN outperforms the vanilla PINN and its certain variants in prediction accuracy within and beyond the training domain with fewer sampling points, while preserving the underlying finite group properties.

Methods We reviewed 85 consecutive cementless total hip arthroplasties performed between 2002 and 2005 using ArCom non–cross-linked PE liners (Biomet Inc., Warsaw, IN). After excluding 31 hips lost to follow-up and 5 revised hips, 49 hips (45 patients) with ≥20 years of follow-up were analyzed. Femoral head penetration was measured using PolyWare (Draftware Inc., Vevay, IN) by three independent observers. The first postoperative year was defined as the bedding-in phase, and subsequent penetration as the steady-state phase (SSP). Associations between wear and patient, implant, surgical, and clinical factors were assessed. Results The mean Japanese Orthopaedic Association score improved from 39.6 ± 10.6 preoperatively to 84.4 ± 12.9 at 20 years ( P < .001). Osteolysis was observed in 18 hips. Mean bedding-in phase and SSP wear rates were 0.235 ± 0.155 mm/y and 0.031 ± 0.023 mm/y, respectively. SSP wear correlated linearly with postoperative time (R 2 = 0.99). Hips with higher SSP wear (>0.025 mm/y) had higher 20-year Japanese Orthopaedic Association gait ( P = .033), activities of daily living ( P = .018), and total scores ( P = .013). Charnley category A had higher SSP wear than category B ( P = .024), whereas osteolysis did not affect wear rates. Conclusions ArCom conventional PE showed a nearly constant SSP wear rate over 20 years. Exploratory analyses suggested associations with functional status and Charnley category, but not with other patient, implant, or surgical factors.

The secondary outcome measure was total oral morphine consumption from PACU discharge to postoperative day 1 (POD#1), expressed in oral morphine equivalents (OME). papers.title: MLP-Based Condition Assessment Method for Marine Propulsion Shafting Driven by Measured and Digital Twin Data Fusion
papers.abstract: Marine propulsion shafting operates under complex, variable conditions, where stern bearing wear and pedestal settlement redistribute loads, migrate vibration energy, and distort the shaft orbit, threatening safe operation. To address insufficient fault samples, difficulty in measuring degradation states directly, and limited interpretability of purely data-driven models, we propose a multilayer perceptron (MLP) condition assessment method driven by measured and digital twin data fusion. A digital twin framework comprising geometric, physical, rule-based, and behavioral models was constructed. A Timoshenko beam finite element model and modal truncation reduce computational cost while describing displacement-induced load and vibration responses. Static and dynamic tests are performed on a shafting test rig, and condition matching, outlier processing, and feature-level fusion produce a dual-source dataset. The MLP takes rotational speed, support forces of the four bearings, and normalized temporal position as input features; temperature scaling calibrates the class probabilities, while a separate severity score indicates the condition trend. The reduced model maintains first three natural-frequency errors below 10% and representative bearing-load errors below 5%. On an independent temporal hold-out test set, the MLP achieves 96.78% accuracy and 87.96% fault recall. Within the tested laboratory-scale, settlement-dominated operating range, these results demonstrate an effective and physically interpretable approach for condition assessment and risk early warning of marine propulsion shafting.

papers.abstract: Background Accurate perioperative risk prediction remains challenging because of class imbalance, cohort heterogeneity, unstable probability estimates and limited interpretability. Objective To develop and externally evaluate CardioMonoStack, an ensemble architecture integrating heterogeneous base learners, branch-level monotonicity priors, stacked meta-learning and feature-dependent residual logit correction. Methods We conducted a multicentre retrospective cohort study of 1911 patients aged ≥65 years undergoing total hip arthroplasty across five healthcare databases. CardioMonoStack was developed using MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, validated in INSPIRE, and externally tested in eICU and MOVER. Performance was assessed using AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, threshold-dependent classification measures, calibration plots and decision curve analysis. Interpretability was examined using SHAP, interaction and individual conditional expectation analyses. Results CardioMonoStack achieved the highest AUROC point estimates among evaluated models in eICU (0.790; 95% CI 0.711–0.865) and MOVER (0.866; 95% CI 0.761–0.949), with AUPRC values of 0.569 (95% CI 0.415–0.717) and 0.571 (95% CI 0.328–0.792), respectively. Calibration and net benefit varied across cohorts and comparators. Omission of L3 increased Brier-score and log-loss point estimates in both external cohorts; paired confidence intervals supported these differences in MOVER but were inconclusive in eICU. SHAP analyses prioritised blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, age, and metabolic and demographic factors. Conclusion CardioMonoStack is a candidate framework for estimating in-hospital heart-failure risk after total hip arthroplasty. Despite promising external discrimination, prospective validation, local recalibration, and clinical impact evaluation are required before implementation.

papers.title: Hydrogel and scaffold strategies for talar osteochondral repair: biofabrication, ankle biomechanics, and clinical translation
papers.abstract: Osteochondral lesions of the talus combine focal cartilage injury with variable subchondral bone damage in a small, highly loaded joint, making successful biomaterial translation dependent on more than regenerative capacity alone. This review examines hydrogel, scaffold, and biofabrication strategies for talar osteochondral repair through the combined lenses of ankle biomechanics, spatial construct design, and clinical feasibility. Defect containment, shoulder involvement, cystic depth, instability, and alignment alter the requirements for conformal filling, wet-field retention, cyclic compression and shear tolerance, and cartilage-bone anchorage. Recent biofabrication approaches, including gradient and multilayer scaffolds, 3D-printed architectures, decellularized extracellular-matrix hydrogels, directional microchannels, and adhesive or bioactive systems, provide increasing control over spatial organization and mechanical transitions, but most remain preclinical. Human studies support the feasibility of matrix- and scaffold-assisted talar repair, including autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis, collagen- and hyaluronic acid-based platforms, cell-supported constructs, and related one-step procedures; however, heterogeneous lesion selection, concomitant bone grafting, instability correction, rehabilitation, imaging, and follow-up limit direct material-level comparisons. The central translational question is whether a material architecture addresses the dominant mechanical and surgical requirements of a defined talar lesion. Evaluation should therefore integrate wet-field handling, edge and interface stability, cyclic loading, bone-side integration, degradation under load, manufacturing reproducibility, and lesion-stratified clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Crosslinking-controlled biopolymer biomaterials for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine: network chemistry, processing, and mechanistically informed validation
papers.abstract: Crosslinking is often treated as a technical step used to stabilize biopolymer scaffolds, yet in regenerative biomaterials it is a primary design variable that simultaneously controls network mechanics, viscoelasticity, swelling, molecular transport, degradation, ligand accessibility, and cell–material interactions. This Review examines crosslinked biopolymer biomaterials for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine through that network-centered perspective. Collagen and gelatin, hyaluronic acid, silk fibroin, chitosan, alginate, fibrin, and related matrices are considered with emphasis on how covalent, photoinduced, enzymatic, ionic, physical, and dynamic covalent crosslinking generate distinct biological microenvironments. We analyze how crosslinking is coupled to processing routes including extrusion bioprinting, electrospinning, freeze-drying, injectable hydrogel formation, and porous-scaffold fabrication, and why the timing of network formation can be as important as nominal polymer composition. We propose a mechanistically informed evidence chain connecting material definition to hydrated-state properties, cellular response, ex vivo or in vivo behavior, and tissue-specific regenerative outcomes. Particular attention is given to quantitative network characterization, reproducibility, sterilization, storage, aging-related property drift, and controls needed to distinguish genuine network effects from formulation confounders. Clinical trials, patient data, patent landscapes, regulatory pathways, commercialization, and product-development strategies are intentionally excluded. Crosslinking should be designed and reported as a multidimensional regulator of the regenerative microenvironment rather than as a single measure of scaffold stability.

papers.title: Cold atmospheric plasma as a perioperative adjunct in oral surgery: A narrative review of surface activation, decontamination and soft‐tissue healing
papers.abstract: Abstract Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) is a non‐thermal ionised gas that generates reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and can modify titanium surface chemistry, inactivate oral pathogens and modulate soft‐tissue repair at temperatures compatible with living tissue. This narrative review synthesises evidence identified through a structured multi‐database search, organised around three points in oral surgical care: pre‐treatment activation of titanium devices, intraoperative decontamination in peri‐implant, periodontal and endodontic surgery, and postoperative oral wound management. For activation, CAP lowers the titanium contact angle and increases osteoblast attachment in vitro and in animals, with early human studies reporting improved implant stability on a surrogate endpoint. For decontamination, CAP disrupts biofilm in vitro but has not consistently outperformed sodium hypochlorite and lacks any surgical trial. For wound care, two controlled human trials, one of them randomised, report accelerated oral epithelialisation, whereas an analgesic effect is inconsistent. The three applications share a common platform but differ in reactive‐species profile, parameters and level of evidence, which stays preclinical for most and clinical only on surrogate endpoints. Standardised multidimensional dosimetry and randomised trials with definitive endpoints remain the principal unmet needs before CAP can be recommended as a routine adjunct in oral surgery.

papers.abstract: Lattice structures are increasingly used in lightweight engineering applications, particularly in the aerospace, biomedical, and automotive sectors. However, their limited stiffness and narrow linear elastic region can restrict their use in load-bearing applications. This study investigates a hybrid design strategy for improving the compressive performance of Ti-6Al-4V octet lattice structures generated in polar coordinates. Hybrid lattices incorporating a 0.5 mm outer and inner tubular shell and reference lattices without a shell were designed using implicit modeling techniques and manufactured by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The mechanical response was characterized through uniaxial compression testing showing an increase in the compressive strength of 900 to 1000% and a strength-to-weight ratio similar to that of bulk titanium in the case of the hybrid samples. Geometrical analysis revealed systematic manufacturing deviations, with all lattice struts exhibiting larger diameters than their nominal dimensions. The hybrid design significantly increased the compressive modulus and yield strength while introducing a moderate increase in mass. Furthermore, the as-printed quality of the polar-generated lattices followed trends reported for equivalent Cartesian-coordinate lattice structures or produced even better results. Overall, the results demonstrate that hybridization can increase compressive strength and modulus significantly while improving the strength-to-weight ratio, with polar lattices exhibiting geometry-dependent trends consistent with Cartesian structures and curved-cell designs providing more uniform volume filling and improved suitability for axisymmetric components.

papers.title: Preoperative nutritional status and its association with postoperative complications and survival in patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty: a retrospective cohort analysis
papers.abstract: Background Adverse preoperative nutritional indicators are common among patients undergoing hip arthroplasty and have been associated with poorer surgical outcomes. However, evidence simultaneously evaluating multiple preoperative nutritional measures in relation to short-term postoperative complications and longer-term survival in patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty remains limited. Objective To evaluate the associations of preoperative nutritional status, assessed using the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), serum albumin, and Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 (NRS-2002), with 30-day postoperative complications and overall survival in patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty (THA). Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study enrolled 426 consecutive patients who underwent primary THA between January 2020 and December 2023 at a tertiary academic medical center. Patients were stratified into three preoperative PNI strata: PNI ≥ 45 ( n = 198), PNI 40–44.9 ( n = 142), and PNI < 40 ( n = 86). The primary outcomes were 30-day postoperative complications and estimated 3-year overall survival. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to explore adjusted associations. Results The overall 30-day complication rate was 18.3% (78/426). Patients with PNI < 40 had a significantly higher complication rate (34.9%) than those with PNI 40–44.9 (19.0%) and PNI ≥ 45 (10.6%; p < 0.001). In the reported adjusted model, PNI < 40 (OR = 3.42, 95% CI: 2.01–5.82; p < 0.001), serum albumin < 35 g/L (OR = 2.64, 95% CI: 1.58–4.41; p < 0.001), and NRS-2002 score ≥ 3 (OR = 2.21, 95% CI: 1.35–3.62; p = 0.002) were associated with higher odds of postoperative complications. The estimated 3-year overall survival probabilities were 93.4, 82.4, and 68.6% for the PNI ≥ 45, PNI 40–44.9, and PNI < 40 strata, respectively (log-rank p < 0.001). In the reported Cox model, PNI < 40 was associated with higher mortality (HR = 2.96, 95% CI: 1.78–4.92; p < 0.001). Conclusion Lower preoperative PNI, hypoalbuminemia, and NRS-2002-defined nutritional risk were associated with higher postoperative complication risk and lower estimated long-term survival after THA. These measures may assist preoperative risk stratification. Prospective studies are required to determine whether nutritional interventions modify postoperative complications or survival.

papers.title: Physics-prior-guided stress concentration factor prediction for marine engine crankshaft
papers.abstract: To address the computational cost of finite element analysis and the small-sample boundary extrapolation distortion of data-driven surrogate models, an additive residual prediction framework (ARPF) integrating classification society empirical priors is proposed for predicting crankshaft transition fillet stress concentration factors (SCFs). The ARPF utilizes an analytical empirical formulation as a macroscopic baseline to explicitly de-trend the response space, compressing target physical residuals into a stationary, narrow interval and substantially reducing regression complexity. Five surrogate paradigms were evaluated across sample sizes from N = 25 to 250 against an independent test set. Under the small-sample regime of N = 50, direct prediction exhibited localized error spikes, with maximum relative errors (MaxRE) of random forest and support vector regression reaching 25.81% and 24.53%, respectively. In contrast, the ARPF improved the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of all five models to above 0.996 and restricted MaxRE below 13%. Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and non-parametric effect sizes across ten scrambled Sobol repetitions confirmed the robustness of these accuracy gains. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the prior-anchored macroscopic monotonic trend suppresses boundary extrapolation divergence, reliably supporting structural optimization with minimal finite element evaluations.

papers.title: Categorical optimization via Bayesian anchored latent trust-regions for structural design under high-dimensional uncertainties
papers.abstract: Categorical structural optimization under aleatoric uncertainties presents significant challenges due to the requirement of selecting each design variable from a finite catalog of allowable instances. Moreover, each candidate design necessitates costly stochastic finite-element evaluations. Existing latent-space optimization methods, while capable of reducing the dimensionality of catalog attributes, typically treat the resultant space as a continuous search domain. This approach necessitates rounding off the continuous optimum to the nearest catalog instance, potentially altering the objective value, constraint status, or physical interpretation of the design. To mitigate this issue, this paper introduces the Categorical Optimization with Bayesian Anchored Latent Trust-Regions (COBALT) framework, designed for high-dimensional categorical optimization under uncertainties (OUU). COBALT initially embeds the physical catalog into a low-dimensional latent representation, locking the mapped instances as a discrete anchored graph. Subsequently, a data-independent random tree decomposition is employed to offer bounded-complexity additive modeling for high-dimensional categorical variables. On this anchored domain, an additive Sparse Axis-Aligned Subspace Gaussian Process (SAAS-GP) surrogate is fitted to heteroscedastic Monte Carlo-based Finite Element Analysis (MC-FEA) observations. A trust-region discrete graph acquisition search is then used to select the next admissible catalog configuration, avoiding continuous relaxation or rounding-off. The proposed strategy is demonstrated in the robust design optimization of complex beam structures, considering factors such as structural weight, strain energy, and local buckling performance. Numerical examples indicate that evaluating only valid catalog designs through the MC-FEA oracle preserves physical admissibility throughout the active learning loop. Furthermore, it can enhance the efficiency of robust categorical structural optimization when compared to relaxation-based and non-surrogate search strategies under equivalent conditions.

papers.title: Porosity-Tunable Zn-0.5Mg Triply Periodic Minimal Surface Scaffolds Enable Immune-Osteogenic Coupling for Customized Bone Regeneration
papers.abstract: Abstract Bone defects remain a clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of native bone and the lack of biodegradable implants capable of actively regulating the healing microenvironment. Current metallic scaffolds often suffer from an intrinsic trade-off among mechanical properties, degradation behavior, and bioactivity, limiting their therapeutic efficacy in load-bearing bone regeneration. Herein, porosity-tunable Zn-0.5Mg scaffolds with a triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structure are fabricated via selective laser melting. By systematically varying scaffold porosities (40, 60, and 80%), the coordinated regulation of mechanical properties, degradation performance, and ion release is achieved. The incorporation of Mg into Zn-0.5Mg enhances mechanical strength and stabilizes degradation behavior, while increasing the porosity accelerates Zn and Mg ion release in a controllable manner. Importantly, the co-released ions promote macrophage polarization, thereby establishing an immunoregulatory microenvironment favorable for bone regeneration. In a rabbit femoral condyle defect model, the implantation of Zn-0.5Mg scaffolds with high porosity (80%) enhanced bone ingrowth into interconnected pore networks and accelerated new bone formation over 14 weeks, without inducing systemic toxicity. Overall, this study establishes a porosity-tunable and immune-osteogenic coupling strategy in biodegradable Zn-0.5Mg scaffolds, offering a generalizable design for customizable and bioactive bone implants.

The bar diameter is varied parametrically from 19 mm to 28 mm, and three materials (26MnB5 steel, Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy, and Al7075-T6 aluminum alloy) are considered to evaluate the influence of shear modulus. Modal behavior is evaluated using an equivalent linearized representation of the bushings. The results show that torsional stiffness increases with both the diameter and the material shear modulus, consistent with theoretical expectations. At the same time, the absolute values are affected by geometry and bushing compliance. The review focused on implant materials and surface characteristics, osteoblast adhesion, proliferation, differentiation, mineralised matrix formation, vitamin D biology, and clinical evidence related to vitamin D and dental implant osseointegration. Results Current evidence indicates that implant surface characteristics, including roughness, topography, surface chemistry, hydrophilicity, and coatings, influence osteoblast behaviour and the biological response at the bone-implant interface. Titanium remains the most established implant material, while zirconia and titanium-zirconium alloys have shown favourable biological and clinical performance in selected indications. Vitamin D is known to be biologically relevant for bone metabolism and osteoblast activity, and experimental studies suggest that it may support osteogenic differentiation and mineralised matrix formation. However, current human clinical evidence regarding vitamin D and implant outcomes remains limited and heterogeneous. Conclusions Osseointegration is influenced by a complex interaction between implant material characteristics, surface properties, osteoblast responses, systemic vitamin D status, and host-related biological factors. Although vitamin D is known to be biologically relevant and experimental findings are promising, there is currently insufficient evidence to show that vitamin D has variable effects on osseointegration around titanium, zirconia, or titanium-zirconium implants. Further in vitro, in vivo, and clinical studies are needed using clearly defined implant materials, surface characteristics, vitamin D status or supplementation protocols, and clinical outcomes.

The optimization process is subject to constraints ensuring that the target lifetime of selected turbine components is met, considering varying inflow conditions. This results in optimal control setpoints for each turbine as functions of ambient conditions. After introducing the economic lifetime-aware WFC approach, the paper analyzes two case studies. The benefits of the proposed methodology are highlighted by comparing it to a range of reference control strategies, which either ignore component damage or address fatigue loads in alternative simplified ways. When compared to greedy and power-maximizing WFC strategies, results show that only the lifetime-aware formulation ensures the achievement of the desired lifetime targets. papers.title: Methane Emissions in Melbourne, Australia. Part 2: Improving Prior Estimates Using Synthesis Inversion
papers.abstract: Abstract Urban methane emissions remain highly uncertain due to the complexity of overlapping anthropogenic sources and limitations in current bottom‐up inventories. In this study, we apply a synthesis inversion framework to refine sector‐specific methane emissions for the Melbourne region in Australia, using in situ atmospheric observations and a Bayesian inversion approach. Our method incorporates constrained and unconstrained inversions, observational filtering, and ensemble‐based uncertainty quantification, including both ensemble spread and posterior covariance structure. The inversion indicates that prior methane emissions are substantially underestimated, particularly for emissions from gas infrastructure, which are inferred to be approximately five to seven times larger than prior estimates. Posterior emission estimates show substantial improvements in agreement with observations, as evidenced by reduced root mean square error (RMSE), increased correlation, and lower model bias across five receptor sites. Posterior methane emissions for the Melbourne region range from 222 to 253 kt/year across the six study months, representing a 67%–90% increase relative to the prior inventory of 133.5 kt/year. Sensitivity analyses confirm that these total emission estimates are robust to prior perturbations and inversion configuration choices. However, source attribution remains sensitive in cases of spatial overlap or low observational coverage. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of synthesis inversion in urban methane quantification and highlights its value for supporting targeted mitigation strategies and improving emission reporting in urban Australia.

Relative to the equiatomic baseline they show 27–28% higher ductility and a 32% higher strength–ductility product over 298–873 K. Nucleation proceeds by stress-induced homogeneous shear without a dislocation precursor, and the transformation reverts almost completely on unloading via Shockley partials. papers.title: A hybrid artificial intelligence framework for three-dimensional electromagnetic field mapping using airborne measurements in general aviation
papers.abstract: The increasing electrification of aircraft systems and development of autonomous aviation technologies increase the need for accurate characterization of electromagnetic field (EMF) distributions under operational conditions. However, dense three-dimensional EMF measurements in aviation environments are difficult to obtain because airborne observations are typically sparse, irregularly distributed, and collected under varying flight conditions. Here, we present an artificial intelligence-based framework for three-dimensional reconstruction of the electric field component of EMF from real-world airborne measurements in general aviation. The study uses more than 80 h of measurements collected during operational activities involving four aircraft types and a low-cost, high-sensitivity sensing platform recording synchronized electric-field and geospatial data over the 1-8000 MHz frequency range. Geostatistical and machine-learning approaches, including Kriging, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and Exact Gaussian Processes, were evaluated for three-dimensional field reconstruction. Based on this comparison, we developed a hybrid Deep Gaussian Process Kolmogorov-Arnold Feature Extractor (DGKAN), combining nonlinear feature representation with probabilistic spatial modeling and uncertainty estimation. DGKAN achieved the highest predictive accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 0.0381 and a mean squared error of 0.0071, reducing the mean absolute error by approximately 27.6% relative to the strongest baseline model. These results demonstrate that combining Kolmogorov-Arnold representations with probabilistic Gaussian Process modeling enables accurate reconstruction of three-dimensional electromagnetic field distributions from sparse airborne measurements. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach for electromagnetic environment assessment in general aviation and establishes a basis for further development of intelligent EMF monitoring and prediction methods under operational flight conditions.

papers.title: Tool life prediction integrating cutting power: a comparative analysis of machine learning models
papers.abstract: Abstract Monitoring and predicting tool wear remains a critical challenge in hard turning operations because it directly affects process efficiency, surface integrity, and manufacturing sustainability. Although cutting power is readily available in industrial environments, its potential as an indirect indicator of tool condition and an auxiliary predictor of tool life remains limited. This study proposes a Machine Learning (ML) framework that integrates cutting power consumption with machining parameters to improve tool life prediction in the dry turning of hardened AISI 52,100 steel using mixed ceramic inserts. A Central Composite Design with three factors (cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut) was employed. Several ML surrogate models optimized through Bayesian Optimization were evaluated under three predictive scenarios: (i) machining parameters predicting tool life ( T ); (ii) machining parameters predicting cutting power ( Pc ); and (iii) machining parameters combined with Pc predicting T. In general, the inclusion of cutting power contributed to improved predictive performance, reducing errors for some of the evaluated models. Gaussian Process Regression achieved the best overall performance for tool life prediction (RMSE = 0.6998) in Scenario 3, whereas Artificial Neural Networks provided the best power prediction (RMSE = 0.1583) in Scenario 2. The results demonstrate that low-cost cutting power can act as a reliable indirect indicator of tool condition, enabling more accurate tool life prediction without additional sensor infrastructure. This approach supports sustainable and efficient machining operations by balancing productivity and resource conservation while avoiding premature tool replacement and the energy waste associated with using worn tools.

papers.title: Delayed arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement may negatively impact postoperative improvement and return to sport: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a common clinical syndrome with a high prevalence among athletes. Arthroscopy for FAI boasts excellent patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and return to sport (RTS), but predictors of outcomes have been identified. Existing studies suggest that delayed arthroscopy may be associated with inferior PROs, but evidence for sport-specific outcomes is lacking. Aim Our aim was to analyze the impact of timing on (i) postoperative outcomes and (ii) return to sport following primary hip arthroscopy for FAI through a systematic review. Methods Our systematic review queried Pubmed, Embase, and Cochrane Library. Studies examining patients aged 16 or older underdoing primary arthroscopy for FAI that stratified outcomes based on time to surgery were included. Studies that were unavailable in English, not primary research, or analyzing revision procedures or FAI secondary to other lesions were excluded. The heterogeneity inherent to the populations studied precluded meta-analysis. Results Of 849 studies identified, 24 met inclusion criteria, representing a population of 23 742. Late surgery was associated with lower rates of RTS, RTS at lower play levels, and lower HOS-SS scores but not with time to RTS. Studies reported inferior improvements in non-sport PROs in delayed arthroscopy compared to earlier intervention. Later surgery was associated with greater postoperative opioid use and greater rates of total hip arthroplasty. Conclusions Delayed arthroscopy for FAI may be associated with inferior sport-related outcomes and improvements in PROs compared to earlier intervention. Substantial heterogeneity existed between the included studies, but these associations were consistent across analytic methods.

papers.title: Physics-Guided Machine Learning Approach for Roughness Prediction in Jointed Plain Concrete Pavements
papers.abstract: The International Roughness Index (IRI) is a crucial indicator of rigid pavement performance and distress, and artificial neural networks (ANNs) have made pavement management system (PMS) forecasting more cost-effective. However, purely data-driven ANN models are not constrained to follow known physical trends and can behave unpredictably outside their training range. This study developed a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for predicting IRI in jointed plain concrete pavements (JPCPs) by incorporating an empirical equation from the Mechanistic-Empirical Pavement Design Guide (MEPDG) into the training loss, intended to bias predictions toward physically consistent trends. A total of 2705 observations from 394 U.S. and 6 Canadian pavement sections were used to train the model and compare it against a conventional ANN, standard regression, and the standalone MEPDG equation. The PINN achieved a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.695 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 11.79 in./mi. Its performance was comparable to the ANN (R2 = 0.698, RMSE = 11.71 in./mi), and both outperformed the MEPDG equation and conventional regression. A closed-form equation was extracted from the trained ANN weights and biases. While the physics constraint did not improve predictive accuracy in this study, it offers a transparent, interpretable tool that agencies can apply directly to prioritize JPCP maintenance and rehabilitation without proprietary model files.

papers.title: Targeting G protein-coupled receptor networks for healthy aging: grounding systems geroprotection in biophysical and data realities
papers.abstract: In their lead article in Frontiers in Science, Boeringer et al. propose targeting networks of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) as a promising strategy for geroprotection (Boeringer et al. 2026). This approach builds on the remarkable versatility of GPCRs, which sense a wide range of extracellular signals, engage diverse signaling pathways, are broadly expressed across tissues, and play important roles in many disease processes. By framing the GPCRome as a central, druggable regulator of multiple hallmarks of aging, from inflammaging and mitochondrial dysfunction to stem cell depletion, the authors advance an intriguing hypothesis in which systems pharmacology could be used to rebalance several of these processes simultaneously, potentially delaying the onset of chronic disease and extending healthspan. The proposed integration of artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and quantum computing to rationally manipulate such complex signaling networks is bold and thought-provoking.At the same time, translating this compelling vision into therapeutic reality presents formidable biophysical, computational, and experimental challenges. The authors explicitly acknowledge several of these limitations, including the sparsity and variable quality of available training data, the context dependence of GPCR signaling, and, importantly, the fact that network-and AI-guided polypharmacology does not yet constitute a validated or generalizable framework for designing multi-receptor interventions. Several further considerations may help define what will be required to move this exciting concept from a compelling systems-level hypothesis toward an experimentally testable and ultimately translatable framework for GPCR network pharmacology.The proposed networks contain many receptors with established disease relevance, but deciding that a receptor belongs in an aging network does not tell us how it should be modulated. A therapeutic network requires knowing whether a receptor should be activated, inhibited, partially activated, allosterically modulated, biased toward one effector, or manipulated in a tissue-restricted manner, and by how much. This distinction matters because GPCR effects are strongly dependent on receptor density, coupling repertoire, accessory proteins, cellular state, ligand concentration, and tissue context.Especially problematic is the situation for biased ligands. Compared with binding data, efficacy data are sparse and functional measurements are not interchangeable across assays.A ligand that appears biased in one cellular background may not retain the same functional preference in another because receptor expression levels, membrane lipid composition, expression reserve, transducer abundance, signal amplification, and regulatory machinery differ. Consequently, pooling efficacy measurements from heterogenous assays may obscure the underlying pharmacology and limit the predictive utility of models trained on such data.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to assemble more data, but to assemble the right data, including their experimental context.The proposed GPCRome is necessarily constrained by measurements reported in the literature. This creates an important circularity: well-studied receptors become highly connected nodes, while poorly characterized receptors, including orphan receptors (i.e., receptors without known endogenous or synthetic ligands) or incompletely deorphanized GPCRs, may be absent or misrepresented despite mediating potentially important biology, leaving major blind spots in any GPCRome network reconstruction. Boeringer et al. also highlight receptors for which human or translational evidence remains limited, with several proposed nodes supported primarily by in vitro cellular assays and animal models. It remains uncertain whether network topologies derived from controlled rodent experiments will reproduce the networks operating in complex, heterogeneous human populations.A useful next step would therefore be a community-wide effort to construct a standardized, machine-readable GPCR functional atlas. But the harder question is what such an atlas should actually measure, as binding affinity alone is insufficient. Harmonized measurements of ligand association and dissociation, receptor expression and activation, G-protein coupling, β-arrestin engagement, pathway-specific efficacy, receptor trafficking and internalization, desensitization, and signaling duration, are urgently needed-ideally across multiple physiologically relevant cellular backgrounds. Rather than reducing heterogeneous experiments to a single activity label, negative results and experimental metadata should be collected as well, and ideally shared in standardized, accessible format. Such a resource could make network inference more robust and, importantly, reveal where uncertainty really lies. While ligands reshape populations of GPCR conformations, different transducers both select receptor states and undergo their own conformational changes. Thus, signaling cannot be reduced to a ligand-induced receptor state. Rather, AI-based structure prediction, molecular dynamics and enhanced sampling, structural biology, and biophysical measurements should be considered complementary approaches for characterizing receptor-transducer conformational ensembles (Wootten et al., 2013;Hilger et al., 2018).Kinetics adds another critical dimension. Ligand residence time, receptor activation and deactivation rates, trafficking and recycling, and the duration of downstream signaling may influence in vivo efficacy and therapeutic window beyond what is captured by equilibrium affinity or endpoint efficacy (Copeland et al., 2006). Incorporating these temporal features into network models could improve both the selection of network-level interventions and the prediction of physiological outcomes.Sparse data should not necessarily halt progress, but they should change the modeling strategy. Transfer learning offers a particularly attractive route: models can learn shared representations from data-rich GPCRs and then adapt to understudied receptors, provided that domain differences and uncertainty are explicitly modeled [e.g., (Provasi and Filizola, 2025)]. The goal should not be to manufacture confidence from sparse data, but to quantify uncertainty and use it to prioritize the next experiment. AI can then become an activelearning engine linking prediction to targeted measurements rather than a one-way generator of hypotheses (Nguyen et al., 2024).A related issue is chemical space. Much of the historical GPCR ligand repertoire was optimized for individual targets, not for deliberately engineered polypharmacology. The chemical matter already available to the field may therefore be a poor representation of the multitarget molecules needed for network control. While generative modeling architectures have successfully enabled the exploration of new regions of chemical space, the objective should be defined in terms of multi-receptor and multi-pathway pharmacology, including selectivity, efficacy, kinetics, tissue exposure, and safety, rather than simply potency at one receptor. This is where structure-based methods, functional profiling, generative chemistry, and experimental validation need to be tightly coupled.Perhaps the most important question is whether the proposed network architecture will have translational relevance. Boeringer et al. (Boeringer et al. 2026) present mechanistic hypotheses that draw largely on cellular studies, animal models, and selected examples of clinical pharmacology. However, networks inferred from preclinical systems may look quite different in patients, where age, genotype, comorbidities, medication history, tissue composition, and disease stage can all reshape signaling. The authors' vision of digital twins and patient-specific GPCR interventions is compelling precisely because it points to this missing layer.The next step should be to test these network hypotheses directly against patient-derived data rather than assume that preclinical networks represent stable therapeutic maps. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, functional biomarkers, clinical phenotypes, and longitudinal treatment-response data could help establish which receptor nodes are conserved in humans and which are specific to particular tissues. Ultimately, the goal should not be to build a larger GPCR network, but a better-calibrated one that makes predictions that can be rigorously tested, challenged, and ultimately falsified in patients.A major strength of the Boeringer et al. article is that it challenges the field to think beyond the single receptor. That is an important conceptual shift. The next challenge is not simply to add more receptors, but to establish the experimental and computational standards needed to make network pharmacology genuinely testable. Such a program would: combine systematic, context-rich functional measurements with patient-derived evidence; use approaches such as transfer learning and uncertainty-aware active learning to deal with sparse data; account for receptor-transducer mechanisms and signaling kinetics rather than relying on static structures alone; and integrate physics-based and data-driven approaches to connect molecular mechanisms with cellular and organismal behavior (Hendrickx et al., 2020).The central question, then, is whether we can generate the data, assays, models, and chemical tools needed to perturb these networks in a predictable way. Turning this framework into something clinically useful will require considerably more experimental grounding and validation than the current computational roadmap implies.diseases might eventually become. But moving from theoretical network diagrams to clinically useful geroprotective therapeutics will require computational models firmly grounded in experimental biophysics and human biology. No single computational or experimental approach will be sufficient. What is needed instead is an integrated framework that brings together community-generated harmonized functional data, kinetic profiling, mechanistic modeling, generative chemistry, and patient-derived evidence. papers.title: Prevalence and functional impact of musculoskeletal pain among university students in seven Arab countries and its sociodemographic and lifestyle associations
papers.abstract: Musculoskeletal pain (MSP) represents a major public health challenge globally, particularly among university students who are in a critical transitional phase of life characterized by intense academic demands, lifestyle changes, and increasing reliance on digital technologies. Sedentary behavior (SB) has been identified as a potential risk factor for MSP; however, evidence from the Arab region remains limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MSP in nine body regions (neck, shoulders, upper back, elbows, wrists/hands, lower back, hips/thighs, knees, and ankles/feet) across four time points (lifetime, past 12 months, past month, and today), to assess the impact of MSP, and examine the association between SB and MSP. A multinational cross-sectional study was conducted among 4300 university students in seven Arab countries (Egypt, Yemen, Iraq, Sudan, Jordan, Syria, and Palestine), using an online Arabic self-administered questionnaire. Convenience and snowball sampling methods were used to recruit eligible study respondents. MSP was assessed using the Arabic version of the Extended Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ-E). SB was assessed using sedentary behavior questionnaire (SBQ). Chi-square tests were used for univariate associations. Binary logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with any MSP in the past 12 months, and to identify predictors of high SB. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The prevalence of MSP in at least one body region was 84.0% (lifetime), 71.3% (past 12 months), and 64.9% (past month). The neck (49.3%) and lower back (37.3%) were the most affected regions in the past 12 months. Among those affected, preventing usual activities (range: 48.8%–71.7%) and taking medication (range: 37.6–48.2%) were the most reported impacts, while hospitalization remained relatively low (3.2–14.2%). Female sex (aOR = 1.98, 95% CI 1.69–2.31), chronic diseases (aOR = 1.90, 95% CI 1.44–2.49), MSP family history (aOR = 1.96, 95% CI 1.56–2.47), moderate SB (aOR = 1.56, 95% CI 1.32–1.84), and high SB (aOR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.16–1.72) were significantly associated with MSP in the past 12 months, while sleeping 6–8 h was protective (aOR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.67–0.92). This study found a high prevalence of MSP among university students in Arab countries, particularly affecting the neck and lower back. Higher SB, chronic diseases, and a family history of MSP were associated with MSP, whereas adequate sleep appeared to be protective. These findings support the need for university-based strategies that reduce prolonged SB and promote musculoskeletal health, including ergonomic education, active breaks, adjustable study stations, and more active learning environments.

papers.title: Taylor-modified Johnson–Cook constitutive model for pure copper produced using PBF-LB with a green laser source
papers.abstract: Green-laser powder bed fusion offers a route to fabricate dense pure-copper components, but process-induced microstructural heterogeneity complicates their dynamic response at very high strain rates. This study combines quasi-static tension and compression tests, dynamic compression tests using a split Hopkinson pressure bar, and Taylor impact tests to calibrate and validate a modified Johnson–Cook constitutive model. The strain-hardening constants A, B, and n were first fitted from quasi-static data, and an initial strain-rate sensitivity coefficient C was estimated from the dynamic compression tests. Because these tests covered strain rates only up to approximately 3 × 103 s−1, finite-element simulations of Taylor impact tests were used to refine C against the residual length and maximum upset diameter of the recovered specimens. The 122 m/s impact condition alone was used to optimize C; the 166 m/s and 204 m/s conditions were reserved for independent validation. The optimized C value was 0.059, compared with an initial C value of 0.037638. The corrected model yielded global relative errors of 0.1596% and 0.1259% for the two validation conditions, respectively. These results show that combining dynamic compression and Taylor impact data improves predictions for green-laser powder-bed-fused copper under the tested build orientation and loading conditions.
